articles.title: Reform UK promises £80bn of cuts to public spending
articles.summary: Speaking at the party's conference, economy spokesman Robert Jenrick says Reform will be the "party of fiscal responsibility".
articles.body:
Reform UK has pledged to cut £80bn of public spending within five years by reducing welfare, net zero policies, overseas aid and the number of civil servants.

Speaking from the party's conference in Birmingham, economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said he would like to cut taxes in Reform's first Budget if it wins power at the next election but would have to "earn the trust" of the markets first.

Reform would be the "party of fiscal responsibility", he said and promised to make "big changes... in a careful way, not a cack-handed way".

Labour said the proposed cuts were "incredibly reckless and could mean vital public services like hospitals, schools and law enforcement are put at risk".

The bulk of Reform's proposed cuts come from its previously announced plans to reduce the welfare budget by £50bn.

£10bn would be saved by cutting net zero programmes while £8bn would come from reducing the civil service and £7.1bn from capping the foreign aid budget.

The party says its immigration policies, including abolishing indefinite leave to remain, would result in further savings.

Does Reform's plan to cut £50bn in welfare spending add up?

Reform plans to scrap indefinite leave to remain for migrants

Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference

Jenrick is due to give a major speech to the conference on Saturday but speaking at a fringe event with journalist Allister Heath, he sought to reassure voters that Reform's policies would be affordable.

He said it was important to "learn the lessons of [former Prime Minister] Liz Truss" who he said "basically went into a sweetie shop, took everything off the shelves and stuck it into a budget".

"Quite rightly the markets reacted very negatively to that."

Jenrick was a health minister in 2022 when Truss's plan to deliver large energy bill subsidies and £45bn of tax cuts shook market confidence in the UK's financial credibility .

Reform has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax but Jenrick suggested that would not be a priority, arguing relatively few people were affected by it.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he said.

He said his party would retain the triple lock - the mechanism which ensures pensions rise by either 2.5%, the rate of inflation or the rate of average earnings, whichever is highest.

The triple lock is estimated to cost £15.5bn per year by 2030 but Jenrick said he could not look pensioners "in the eye" and cut their income "while there is so much waste in the public sector".

He said it would be "fundamentally unfair going to pensions before we have made hard choices elsewhere".

Jenrick has written to investors who hold government debt to set up meetings in London and New York to discuss what fiscal rules he would set with the aim of reducing the cost of borrowing.

The past few days have seen global borrowing costs rise, with the UK's costs increasing to a 28-year high.

Also speaking at the conference, the party's business spokesman Richard Tice set out a number of proposals aimed at increasing house building on brownfield sites - land that has previously been built on.

He said the party would consult on measures including scrapping stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade for homes built on brownfield sites.

Under the proposals, affordable housing requirements would be removed for brownfield developments outside major cities.

The party's policy document says its plans would reduce tax receipts but argued that additional homes built as a result would boost the economy.

Tice has also suggested cutting business rates for high street shops, offsetting the cost by increasing the tax for online retailers.

Reform's conference at the Birmingham NEC comes at the end of a turbulent summer which saw its leader Nigel Farage resign and then re-run in his Clacton constituency in a bid to end questions about a £5m gift he received before becoming an MP.

There is also a police investigation into donations made to the party.

The main business of the conference is expected to take place on Friday and Saturday, with speeches from Farage and other senior figures, as well as an address by the leader of the French far right National Rally party, Jordan Bardella.

articles.title: Canada unveils new $20 bill featuring portrait of King Charles
articles.summary: The vertical banknote features King Charles III, the first new monarch to appear on a Canadian banknote in more than 70 years.
articles.body:
Canada has unveiled a new $20 banknote featuring a portrait of King Charles III, the first new monarch to appear on a Canadian banknote in more than 70 years, following the death of Queen Elizabeth II in 2022.

The banknote was revealed at a Bank of Canada event on Thursday - a "very special day", central bank governor Tiff Macklem said.

A unique feature of the banknote is its vertical orientation. The back shows an image of the Vimy Ridge memorial in France to commemorate Canada's role in World War I.

The Commonwealth nations of New Zealand and Australia have displayed the King on their coins, though Australia has said it will not feature him on banknotes.

Instead, Australia said it will work on releasing a new $5 banknote that pays tribute to "the culture and history" of Indigenous Australians to replace the current design featuring Queen Elizabeth II.

King Charles will not be on new Australia $5 note

King's invitation to Canada sends a message to Trump - and the world

Canada is the first Commonwealth country to put the King on its banknotes outside of Britain since his ascension to the throne.

In addition, it also depicts a floral and leafy tapestry "inspired by the King's lifetime dedication to the environment", according to the Bank of Canada.

Wayne Long, a Liberal MP and secretary of state for the Canada Revenue Agency, said at the unveiling that the symbols on the banknote "serve as a powerful reminder of who we are as a nation and what we value."

Some elements of it were chosen in consultation with an Indigenous advisory council, the central bank added.

It is the second vertical banknote issued in Canada. The first is the $10 bill, depicting Black civil rights advocate Viola Desmond. Its design went on to be selected as best in the world in 2018 by the International Bank Note Society.

The new $20 banknote will enter circulation early next year, said Macklem.

Polling suggests that many Canadians believe the country should end its formal ties to the British monarchy, particularly in the French-speaking province of Quebec.

But the monarchy's popularity received a small bump as tensions rose between Canada and the US, including the ongoing US-Canada trade war and US President Donald Trump's comments about making Canada the "51st state".

Prime Minister Mark Carney invited the King to open Canada's parliament in May - a visit that Carney at the time said "clearly underscores the sovereignty of our country".

The King is Canada's head of state and is represented in Canada by its Governor General Louise Arbour.

articles.title: Meet Jonathan Thai, the 17-year-old from Alpharetta, Georgia whose nonprofit raised $30,000, donated 400 bikes and taught 350 children to ride
articles.summary: US News: A 17-year-old high school student from Alpharetta, Georgia, has built a non-profit organization that has raised over $30,000, distributed 400 bicycles.
articles.body: A 17-year-old high school student from Alpharetta, Georgia, has built a non-profit organization that has raised over $30,000, distributed 400 bicycles and taught hundreds of children how to ride safely. Jonathan Thai, a competitive triathlete and rising high school senior, founded Pedal Forward in early 2025 after a major outdoor retailer shuttered its local community biking programs. Recognizing the gap in accessible cycling instruction for local families, Thai launched free training clinics and equipment drives across his community. His efforts earned him national recognition as the 8,351st Daily Point of Light award winner, a national honour established by Points of Light to celebrate outstanding volunteer service across the United States.Filling a community voidThe inspiration for Pedal Forward arose in January 2025 when outdoor retailer REI discontinued its Experience program, which had previously provided affordable bike training classes. "Something like biking might just look recreational at first glance," Thai told Points of Light in an interview highlighting his recognition. "But it can have such a big impact for a family that doesn't have access to transportation – getting to school, getting groceries, getting to a job." Drawing on his background as a triathlete and his family's history as refugees from the Vietnam War, Thai sought to make cycling accessible to low-income and underserved youth. His parents had instilled in him the importance of community support, prompting him to organize his first official training clinic on the local Greenway Trail in June 2025. To fund equipment and expand operations, Thai forged partnerships with volunteer networks, including the National Charity League and the Young Men's Service League. Through these alliances, Pedal Forward raised $30,000, securing 400 donated bicycles and distributing 500 helmets to participants.Hands-on instruction and national expansionPedal Forward designs its clinics to accommodate children of varying skill levels. Each training camp typically hosts between 35 and 40 children, maintaining a one-to-one ratio of participants to volunteer instructors. For beginners, volunteers temporarily remove the pedals from the bicycles, allowing young riders to master their balance before learning to pedal. Advanced groups take part in guided rides along community trails under the supervision of lead instructors, many of whom are Thai's triathlon teammates. The clinics conclude with practical drills, including cone-weaving exercises and games designed to build spatial awareness and braking control. Since hosting its inaugural session, Pedal Forward has held 12 free clinics, providing direct instruction to more than 350 children. The non-profit has expanded beyond Georgia, establishing active regional chapters in Tennessee and New York to deliver equipment and safety education to children in other states.Going global with Pedal for VietnamBuilding on its domestic momentum, the organization is preparing an international expansion through an initiative titled Pedal for Vietnam. Inspired by his parents' heritage, Thai is organizing a humanitarian mission aimed at supplying more than 300 bicycles to children living in rural areas of Vietnam, where access to personal transport remains a barrier to education. Reflecting on the growth of the organization, Thai emphasized the broader influence of local grassroots action. "The small things that you might not think have much effect have more impact on families and communities than you realize," Thai said. "If you teach one kid how to ride, maybe they go on to teach other kids. Maybe they start something of their own. Everything has a ripple effect."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: To impart nationalistic learning, Bengal to have 1,000 RSS-run schools within a year: Suvendu
articles.summary: India News: KOLKATA: Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari set a target Thursday to establish at least 1,000 schools run by RSS's education wing Vidya Bharati in.
articles.body: KOLKATA: Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari set a target Thursday to establish at least 1,000 schools run by RSS's education wing Vidya Bharati in every district, municipality and panchayat within a year. He also suggested a plan to merge the state's four education departments into one, specifying that there would be no separate administration for madrassa education.Adhikari, who spoke at an event to mark the 74th anniversary of Vidya Bharati at Ramakrishna Mission Institute of Culture, urged the body to shoulder the responsibility of imparting what he termed "nationalistic learning". He invited its brass to the secretariat to meet officials and take the initiative forward.Bengal has 313 such schools. Nationally, Vidya Bharati runs over 12,000 schools and 10,000 Bal Sanskar Kendras. The CM said he wanted the organisation to focus on establishing more schools in Murshidabad and South 24 Parganas, alleging that "more anti-national activities take place" in these districts. The erstwhile TMC govt, he said, polluted the education environment and institutions like Vidya Bharati would need to "help the state come out of this". He accused TMC of even twisting the Bengali syllabus to divide people. "Mother was referred to as 'amma' and not 'ma'... The syllabus was created in such a way that Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's or Swami Vivekananda's lessons remained neglected..."Invoking Syama Prasad Mookerjee's call of "ek desh, ek bidhan, ek nishan, ek pradhan", the CM said it would apply to education, too. "We won't allow an arrangement where the higher education department will look after all universities, while another department will look after Aliah University," he said. Aliah University is currently managed by the state's minority affairs department. "I felicitated the board toppers. Later, the minority affairs department sent a separate file containing the names of 27 Muslim students. I asked why? ... I have already felicitated 20 students, and they include Muslims, Jains and Buddhists."Anand Rao, a Vidya Bharati official, told TOI its schools train students in "bharatiyatwa (Indianness)" as well as puja rituals. Some run till Class 5, others up to classes 8, 10 and 12.The website of Vidya Bharati Akhil Bhartiya Shiksha Sansthan states its vision is "to develop a system of education which would help build a younger generation committed to Hindutva and infused with patriotic fervour".Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Government to allow retrofit devices for polluting trucks & buses
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In a fresh push to curb vehicular pollution, govt will soon allow old polluting trucks and buses to be fitted with retrofit emission-contro.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a fresh push to curb vehicular pollution, govt will soon allow old polluting trucks and buses to be fitted with retrofit emission-control devices (RECDs) that can reduce particulate matter emissions by up to 90% and nitrogen oxide emissions by 60%. Road transport minister Nitin Gadkari announced the measure Thursday, a move that will complement govt's scrappage and replacement programme for ageing heavy vehicles.Speaking at an event organised by Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (Siam), Gadkari said the device, developed from an innovation at IIT-Delhi, has been successfully tested. Once retrofitted in BS-IV, BS-III and older diesel vehicles, it can bring their emissions on a par with BS-VI standards. Similar devices have already been installed in diesel generator sets to reduce pollution. Gadkari said each device is expected to cost around Rs 4,000-5,000.TOI has learnt that to enable the rollout, road transport ministry will soon notify Automotive Industry Standard 228, which will prescribe technical requirements and performance standards for these devices.Gadkari also highlighted India's acute shortage of buses, saying the country has only two buses per 1,000 people, compared with the global benchmark of eight. He stressed the need for innovative public transport solutions in Tier-II, Tier-III and smaller cities, arguing that metro rail projects are often too capital-intensive to be viable in such places.Taking a swipe at bureaucratic resistance, Gadkari referred to the proposed flash-charging articulated bus system in Nagpur and said, "IAS officers think they are the only intelligent people in the country. Politicians may know only how to win elections, but they believe only they have knowledge. They keep creating hurdles, but it is my responsibility to resolve them."Gadkari also reiterated his ministry's plan to introduce a negative points system for traffic violations to crack down on habitual offenders. The proposal, which he announced Wednesday while launching the 'Suraksha' pilot programme for on-the-spot medical diagnosis and counselling of 10 lakh drivers, construction workers and other high-risk workers involved in highway and mining projects, will assign penalty points for every traffic violation. Drivers accumulating points beyond a specified threshold could face suspension or cancellation of their driving licences, he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1993, Taiwan was called “Garbage Island” as only 70% of trash was collected; 33 years later, recycling reached 55% nationwide
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 1993, Taiwan had a trash problem so severe that it was dubbed “Garbage Island”. The country collected only 70 per cent of its waste, while the rest.
articles.body: In 1993, Taiwan had a trash problem so severe that it was dubbed “Garbage Island”. The country collected only 70 per cent of its waste, while the rest was left to pollute the environment through littering or burning. More than three decades later, Taiwan has turned that crisis into one of the world’s most striking recycling transformations, with a nationwide recycling rate of 55 per cent. The change was driven not by one measure but by a system that made households, businesses and government share responsibility for waste. Residents were required to buy official bags for non-recyclable trash, manufacturers and importers helped fund recycling, and households had to sort their waste before collection. Even the trash trucks became part of daily life, with yellow vehicles playing classical music to signal their arrival. Together, these measures helped make recycling a routine part of life and dramatically reduced the amount of waste sent for disposal.Why did Taiwan introduce paid trash bagsUnder the system, residents must buy official blue bags for non-recyclable trash, making disposal a direct cost. According to Rapid Transition Alliance, the bags cost between 3 and 43 cents depending on their size. The policy encouraged people to think more carefully about what they threw away, while waste generation in Taipei fell by 31 per cent between 1997 and 2015, from 1.26kg to 0.87kg per person per day. Taiwan also made businesses responsible for part of the process. Its Extended Producer Responsibility system requires manufacturers and importers to help fund recycling. Rapid Transition says the 1997 “4-in-1 recycling programme” brought together government, manufacturers, consumers and licensed recycling enterprises. Fees paid into the Recycling Fund helped subsidise collection and recycling, spreading responsibility across the production and consumption chain.How do Taiwan’s musical garbage trucks workTaiwan’s trash collection became famous for yellow trucks that play classical music as they travel through neighbourhoods. Residents listen for the trucks and take their trash directly to them rather than leaving bags outside their homes. Taipei has more than 4,000 collection points operating five nights a week, while mobile apps allow residents to track the trucks and receive alerts when they are nearby. The yellow trucks are followed by separate recycling vehicles, encouraging households to sort their waste before collection. Residents separate general trash, raw and cooked food waste, plastic and paper, while food waste can be used for animal feed or compost. The system has also required substantial infrastructure. Rapid Transition reports that the Recycling Fund had purchased more than 1,300 recycling vehicles for municipalities since 1998 and financed 273 storage facilities for 326 municipal collection squads.How did Taiwan raise recycling to 55%These measures helped Taiwan make a dramatic shift from its “Garbage Island” era. The country now has a recycling rate of 55 per cent and recycles 73 per cent of its plastic. Daily waste disposal also fell from 1.14kg per person in 1998 to under 0.4kg by 2015. The change was not simply about collecting more trash; it was about reducing waste and recovering materials before they reached. Paid trash bags encouraged households to limit non-recyclable waste, while sorting made it possible to separate valuable materials and food waste. Producer responsibility helped fund the collection and recycling system, creating a framework in which businesses also contributed to managing the products they put into circulation.Taiwan’s system brought together government agencies, manufacturers, importers, consumers, community groups and private recyclers rather than placing the entire burden on one group. Households had to sort their trash, businesses helped finance recycling, and public funding supported the vehicles and facilities needed to collect materials. More than three decades after Taiwan collected only 70 per cent of its trash, the country had developed a system capable of recycling 55 per cent nationwide.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Israel kills 3 in Gaza as far-right minister plans for Palestinian removals
articles.summary: Israeli drone strike and gunfire kills and injures people across the Gaza Strip despite ‘ceasefire’.
articles.body:
Israeli attacks have killed at least three people and injured several others across Gaza, as Israeli officials push a plan calling for the removal of Palestinians from the Strip.

An Israeli drone strike on Thursday in the Rimal neighbourhood of western Gaza City killed one person and injured several others, medical sources told Al Jazeera reporters on the ground.

The Palestinian Wafa news agency said the Israeli drone had fired at least two missiles at a group of civilians in the neighbourhood.

Separately, two Palestinians were killed and others were injured in the northern town of Beit Lahia when Israeli forces opened fire at a group of Palestinians, Wafa reported.

Nour Khaled, an Al Jazeera reporter in Gaza, said one of the two victims was a 13-year-old child and the other was an adult who was seriously injured in the attack and passed away after being transferred to a medical point.

The Israeli military meanwhile claimed that its forces had identified two “terrorists who crossed the Yellow Line” in northern Gaza, who they then “eliminated in order to remove the threat they posed”. The so-called Yellow Line is a buffer zone within Gaza established as part of the “ceasefire”.

The ongoing Israeli attacks come despite a United States-brokered “ceasefire” that came into effect in October.

Although major fighting halted in the strip after the agreement, deadly Israeli strikes have continued.

Israeli plan to remove Palestinians from Gaza

While Israeli attacks continue, Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir revealed on Thursday a plan for the removal of the roughly two million Palestinians from the Gaza Strip within seven years.

According to his office, Ben-Gvir’s plan aims to establish a dedicated ministry, as well as secure agreements with countries to take in people from Gaza.

The initiative foresees the departure of 250,000 people in the first year, some 1.1 million within three years and around 1.9 million within seven years, the far-right minister said.

Ben-Gvir said the plan is “realistic” and sought to “encourage the emigration of Gaza’s inhabitants” as a solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz admitted on Wednesday that Israel is still working to remove Palestinians from Gaza.

Forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.

Israeli attacks have already internally displaced the vast majority of Gaza’s people since the start of the genocidal war in Gaza in October 2023.

Israel’s offensive has since claimed at least 73,470 lives in Gaza since then, with more than killed 1,330 since the ceasefire began, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.

articles.title: Ten injured in Ukraine as Kyiv expects talks with US envoys in coming days
articles.summary: Separately, one person killed and five injured after Ukrainian drone struck bus in Russian-controlled part of Horlivka.
articles.body:
At least 10 people have been injured in a Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he expects talks with United States envoys in the coming days.

Kyiv’s military administration said on Thursday that 10 people, including a child, had been injured in the evening attack, while Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the injured included six medical personnel.

The military administration initially said one person had died in the attack, but later said the report had proved untrue.

In a message on Telegram, Klitschko said that the ninth floor of a high-rise residence had been damaged, adding that 15 people had been evacuated from the building in a district just outside the city centre.

Video published on unofficial Telegram channels showed a large fireball rising skywards. Unofficial channels said the building had been struck by a jet-powered drone.

Local media said new explosions later jolted the city. An air raid alert remained in effect more than two hours after it was imposed.

Klitschko said six people had been wounded in earlier strikes on the capital, which has been subject to more than a week of sustained attacks.

Ukraine’s state oil and gas company Naftogaz announced that Russia also attacked its production sites. In a statement, it said the attack caused significant damage to equipment, though it did not give a location.

Meanwhile, one person was killed and five others injured after a Ukrainian drone struck a bus in Horlivka in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s Donetsk region, reported the Interfax news agency.

The bus was hit in “a targeted drone attack”, Interfax said, citing Ivan Prikhodko, the city’s Russian-installed mayor.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the assertion. Ukraine and Russia both deny targeting civilians.

One person was killed and four others injured in a separate drone attack on a passenger bus in Russia’s Belgorod region, local authorities reported.

The attacks came as Zelenskyy said he hoped to host US President Donald Trump’s envoys in Kyiv in the coming days to resume efforts to end the Russian invasion.

Diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year war on Ukraine have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted its focus towards its war in the Middle East.

“We expect to see the envoys of the president of America here in Kyiv. We have confirmation from them,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.

“They will have meetings in Moscow and in Kyiv. We are counting on a meeting in the coming days,” he added.

Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, have been involved in shuttle diplomacy between Russia and Ukraine.

While they have travelled to Moscow multiple times, they have never been to Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said that “tentative dates have been set” for the envoys’ first visit to the Ukrainian capital.

In July, Zelenskyy said he had spoken with Witkoff and Kushner “to reinvigorate diplomacy and bring peace closer”.

Russia’s war on Ukraine has turned into Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, killing thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of troops since 2022.

articles.title: ‘America truly is the best country in the world’: Sri Lankan-origin entrepreneur Chamath Palihapitiya's message on turning 50
articles.summary: US News: Sri Lankan-born investor and entrepreneur Chamath Palihapitiya marked his 50th birthday with a deeply personal message to his children and a powerful .
articles.body: Sri Lankan-born investor and entrepreneur Chamath Palihapitiya marked his 50th birthday with a deeply personal message to his children and a powerful tribute to the United States, the country he credits with giving him the opportunity to build a new life. Reflecting on his journey from growing up as a refugee in Canada to becoming a prominent Silicon Valley investor, Palihapitiya said his life would have been almost unimaginable to his parents when he was born in Sri Lanka in 1976.“I was born in Sri Lanka in 1976 in a country that, at the time, was about to enter a decades long civil war,” he wrote in a post shared on X.His father, who was stationed at the Sri Lankan High Commission in Canada, eventually sought refugee status after his life was threatened by militants. The family remained in Canada as refugees and, according to Palihapitiya, struggled financially. “We grew up on welfare,” he said, crediting his mother for holding the family together and continuing to move forward despite their circumstances.Palihapitiya also recalled starting work at Burger King at the age of 14, handing his wages to his parents to help support the family. One of his responsibilities, he said, was earning enough to help pay for their bus passes because they could not afford a car.Describing himself as a “loser” during his childhood, Palihapitiya said he eventually got his act together in his final year of school and gained admission to a “great university”. After graduating, he immigrated to the US and said he found an opportunity that changed the trajectory of his life.That experience forms the heart of his message about America.“Only in America is this possible,” Palihapitiya wrote, describing how he worked, paid taxes and remained in California because of his loyalty to the opportunities the state had provided him despite its problems.“I found my wife here. Had my kids here. Found my tribe here,” he said.Palihapitiya acknowledged that his journey was not without setbacks. He referred to deaths, divorce, financial difficulties and mistakes he had made along the way. But his advice was not to become consumed by those experiences. “Learn from them. Respect them. BUT MOVE ON,” he wrote.The entrepreneur then turned his reflection into an assertion of the American Dream.“We forget often and try to convince others it’s not true but America truly is the best country in the world,” he wrote. “Everything and anything is possible here. I can testify. Be grateful to be here.”For Palihapitiya, America's appeal is not ultimately about wealth or professional success. He deliberately avoided discussing his accomplishments or fortune in his birthday message, saying those things ultimately “won’t matter”. Instead, he urged his children to focus on things within their control: being kind, having fun, doing meaningful work, finding their community, developing perspective, finding a good partner and living an adventure.“The first 50 years have been that for me - an incredible adventure,” he wrote. Looking ahead to the next half-century, Palihapitiya said he intended to make it another “wild ride”, urging his children to do the same.Chamath Palihapitiya's familyPalihapitiya was married to Brigette Lau until 2018 and they have three children. In 2011, they founded Social Capital, a venture capital firm. Palihapitiya married Nathalie Dompé, an Italian business executive, in 2023. articles.title: ICE agent charged with lying under oath about Minnesota shooting
articles.summary: Authorities say agent fired into home with people inside, lied about circumstances.
articles.body:
Federal prosecutors in the United States have charged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of lying under oath to investigators regarding the shooting of a Venezuelan man during an immigration crackdown this year.

Prosecutors alleged that Christian Castro lied to federal investigators about the events that led up to him firing on 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis through the door of a Minnesota home in January.

The Associated Press news agency and The New York Times reported the indictment, quoting a person familiar with the matter who was not authorised to discuss the investigation publicly. It was expected to be unsealed when Castro is detained.

Castro, a former Department of Homeland Security agent, also faces multiple state felony charges in Minnesota related to the nonfatal shooting, including assault with a dangerous weapon.

Authorities in the Midwestern state had sought to extradite Castro from Texas to face trial. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and President Donald Trump loyalist, declined to cooperate with the request.

The ensuing standoff left Castro detained in Texas for 90 days before his release last week. Under Texas law, the state cannot hold the subject of an extradition order for longer than that. His whereabouts were unclear as of Thursday.

The charges mark a rare move by the Department of Justice under Trump.

Trump’s top officials have repeatedly argued that immigration agents maintain broad protections while conducting enforcement, a position rejected by many legal experts.

For example, no one has been charged in the fatal shootings by immigration agents of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January.

An Associated Press review conducted in February found about two dozen ICE employees and contractors had faced criminal charges since 2020.

An American Civil Liberties Union report released in July documented instances of violent tactics or other civil rights violations in about a third of 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents reviewed in 2025 alone.

The Trump administration distanced itself from the Castro case after video emerged contradicting the agent’s initial accounts of the confrontation.

Castro told investigators that Sosa-Celis had attacked him, which the surveillance footage showed did not happen.

Todd Lyons, then acting head of ICE, said at the time that the footage “has revealed that sworn testimony provided by two separate officers appears to have made untruthful statements”.

Castro and a fellow agent chased Alfredo Aljorna, a Venezuelan national, after a traffic stop, according to charging documents.

Aljorna fled to the home he shared with Sosa-Celis. After a brief scramble, the two men ran inside. Castro then shot through the closed door, “knowing [the home] was occupied by several people”, the documents said.

One witness said there were two children in the house when Castro opened fire. Sosa-Celis was hit in the leg.

Federal authorities have since suspended Castro and dropped all charges against Sosa-Celis and his co-defendant, who were both initially accused of forcibly assaulting an ICE officer. The other agent involved in the incident was also suspended, but has not yet been charged.

Thursday’s indictment comes after ProPublica this week reported that Department of Justice (DOJ) officials had blocked prosecutors from pursuing more serious civil rights charges against Castro, including “deprivation of rights under color of law”.

However, a source close to the investigation told the AP the active investigation could still result in civil rights charges.

The Trump administration has scaled back the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division and dismantled several Biden-era police oversight initiatives since returning to office in January 2025.

That has come as the administration has revved up its mass deportation campaign across the country.

In August, immigration agents detained 50,925 people with the Department of Homeland Security hailing it as a new record for the “highest number of illegal aliens arrested in a single month”.
